info.text: Unit 11 — Reading a wiring diagram and connector/pin talk. Skills-split item bank: listening, reading, use of English, vocabulary.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. Where does wire W241 finally terminate?

generalfeedback.text: The conductor runs from pin 3 on P1, through the harness, and lands on socket B inside connector J12. Pin 3 on P1 is the start, not the end.

feedback.text: Correct — the conductor lands on socket B inside J12.
That is where W241 starts, not where it ends.
TB2 belongs to Dialogue 2's run, not W241 in Dialogue 1.
Pin 4 is the ground/return, not the termination of the signal.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. How does Technician A know the fault is an open circuit and not a short?

generalfeedback.text: An open reads no continuity and an infinite resistance. A short would read near zero resistance to ground — the opposite reading.

answer.text: resistance reads infinite, not near zero

feedback.text: Correct — infinite resistance points to a break, i.e. an open.

answer.text: the circuit breaker keeps tripping to ground

feedback.text: A tripping breaker suggests a short, not an open.

answer.text: the chafed insulation is touching the airframe

feedback.text: That describes a short circuit to ground, the opposite fault.

answer.text: the braided shield is grounding the inner core

feedback.text: That is a short-circuit mechanism, not evidence of an open.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. Technician A says the ground is on pin 4, connected by a bonding strap to the airframe structure.

generalfeedback.text: True. A states: "The ground is on pin 4, connected by a bonding strap to the airframe structure."

feedback.text: Correct — pin 4, via a bonding strap to structure.
Listen again: the ground is on pin 4, bonded to the airframe.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. Technician B reports that the conductor itself is broken.

generalfeedback.text: False. B says the insulation "looks chafed near the clamp, although the conductor itself appears intact." The damage is to the cover, not the wire.

feedback.text: Not quite — the conductor appears intact; only the insulation is chafed.
Correct — the insulation is chafed, but the conductor is intact.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. On which pin number at connector P1 does wire W241 originate? Write the number only.

generalfeedback.text: W241 "originates at pin 3 on connector P1". The answer is 3.

feedback.text: Correct — pin 3 on P1.
Pin 4 is the ground/bonding pin, not the origin.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. Which pin number does Technician B locate — the one he must not confuse with pin 1? Write the number only.

generalfeedback.text: A asks B to "find pin 7 specifically, and be careful not to confuse it with pin 1." The answer is 7.

feedback.text: Correct — pin 7, top row of the socket.
Pin 1 is the one B is warned NOT to confuse it with.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The conductor ends at connector J__. Write the connector number only (for J12, write 12).

generalfeedback.text: The conductor "continues onward to connector J12", and socket B is inside J12. The number is 12.

feedback.text: Correct — connector J12.
P1 is the start connector; the end connector is J12.

questiontext.text:
Read this built-in test (BITE) readout, then answer.

BITE  L/GEAR WARN  CH-A
TEST: CONTINUITY P1(3) - J12(B)
RESULT: NO CONTINUITY
RESISTANCE: OL

What does the reading OL most likely indicate on this run?

generalfeedback.text: OL means over-limit (off the scale) — an infinite resistance. With "no continuity" reported, the path between P1 and J12 is broken: an open circuit.

answer.text: an open circuit on the run

feedback.text: Correct — OL plus "no continuity" means an open circuit.

answer.text: a short circuit to the airframe

feedback.text: A short would read near zero, not OL (infinite).
A good conductor reads a low resistance, not OL.
OL is not a ground reading; it signals no path at all.

questiontext.text:
Read this MEL (Minimum Equipment List) entry, then decide if the statement is true.

MEL 32-61  Gear-down warning lamp (one)
May be inoperative provided the gear-position
indication is confirmed by an alternate means
before each flight. Placard and log required.

Statement: The MEL allows the aircraft to depart with the gear-down warning lamp inoperative, if an alternate means confirms gear position and the defect is placarded and logged.

generalfeedback.text: True. The MEL permits dispatch with the lamp inoperative under the stated conditions: alternate confirmation of gear position, a placard, and a log entry.

feedback.text: Correct — dispatch is allowed under the listed provisions.
Re-read: the entry allows it, provided the conditions are met.

questiontext.text:
Read this note from the Illustrated Parts Catalogue (IPC), then answer.

ITEM 40  CONNECTOR, RECEPTACLE, J12
  Mounts on the equipment rack. Mates with
  plug P/N 812-6 (item 45). Do not order the
  socket contacts separately; see item 50.

According to the note, which part is fixed to the equipment rack?

generalfeedback.text: The receptacle (J12) mounts on the rack. The plug is the moving half that mates with it; the socket contacts sit inside the connector.

feedback.text: Correct — the receptacle is the fixed half on the rack.
The plug is the moving half; it mates with the fixed receptacle.
The socket contacts sit inside the connector, not on the rack.
No bonding strap is mentioned in this IPC note.

questiontext.text:
Read this Service Bulletin extract, then decide if the statement is true.

SB 32-118  Reason: reports of chafed insulation
on harness W2 near the forward clamp, which may
cause an intermittent short to ground. Action:
inspect the routing; add a protective sleeve.

Statement: The bulletin says the chafed insulation may cause an open circuit at the connector.

generalfeedback.text: False. The bulletin warns of an intermittent short to ground from chafed insulation, not an open circuit at the connector.

feedback.text: Not quite — the risk stated is a short to ground, not an open.
Correct — the risk is an intermittent short to ground.

questiontext.text:
Read this work-order step, then answer.

WO 4471  Step 3: Back-probe the mating plug at
P1. Measure continuity from pin 3 through to
socket B at J12. Do not pull on the conductor.

Which action does the step tell the technician to avoid?

generalfeedback.text: The step says "Do not pull on the conductor." Pulling can back out a contact or damage a splice, giving a false open reading.

feedback.text: Correct — the step warns against pulling the conductor.
Back-probing the plug is exactly what the step asks for.
Measuring continuity to socket B is the required test.
Starting at pin 3 is correct; the warning is about pulling.

questiontext.text:
Write the one missing preposition.

"The conductor runs ______ pin 3 on P1 to socket B on J12."

generalfeedback.text: A described path needs from at the start and to at the end. The start is marked by from.

feedback.text: Correct — "from" marks the start of the path.
The start of a path is marked by "from" (from … to …).

questiontext.text:
Write the one missing preposition.

"It travels ______ the harness behind the instrument panel."

generalfeedback.text: Passing inside something long uses through. Watch the spelling: through, not "trough".

feedback.text: Correct — "through" for passing inside the harness.
Use "through" for passing inside the harness.

questiontext.text:
Write the one missing preposition.

"The bonding strap is secured ______ pin 4 of the connector."

generalfeedback.text: A contact or strap sits on or at a pin — never "in" a pin.

feedback.text: Correct — "on pin 4" (or "at pin 4").
Correct — "at pin 4" (or "on pin 4").
Use "on" or "at" a pin, never "in".

questiontext.text:
Write the missing two-word phrase.

"Trace the conductor ______ the plug and follow it downstream."

generalfeedback.text: Leaving the inside of a connector uses out of — the opposite of into.

feedback.text: Correct — "out of the plug".
Use "out of" for leaving the plug (opposite of "into").

questiontext.text: Write the two-word term that means: a complete break in the path, so no current flows.

generalfeedback.text: An open circuit is a complete break. Contrast a short circuit, an unwanted path to ground.

feedback.text: Correct — an open circuit.
Correct — an open circuit.
The term is "open circuit" — a complete break in the path.

questiontext.text:
Write the one missing preposition.

"Run your finger ______ the harness until you reach the clamp."

generalfeedback.text: Following the length of something uses along.

feedback.text: Correct — "along the harness".
Use "along" to follow the length of the harness.

questiontext.text: Write the one word: the hand tool that reads voltage, resistance and continuity.

generalfeedback.text: A multimeter reads voltage, resistance and continuity. You set it to the continuity range before probing.

feedback.text: Correct — a multimeter.
The tool is a "multimeter".

name.text: V1 · connection anatomy — term to meaning

questiontext.text: Match each term to its meaning.

generalfeedback.text: A pin is male, a socket is female, a connector is the whole fitting, and a harness is the bundle of conductors.

correctfeedback.text: All correct — the anatomy of a connection.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some pairs are wrong — check male vs female contact.

incorrectfeedback.text: Re-check: pin = male, socket = female, connector = the whole fitting.

answer.text: the small male contact inside a connector
the female cavity that receives a pin
the fitting that joins two sets of conductors
a bundle of conductors tied together

name.text: V2 · fault and test terms — term to meaning

questiontext.text: Match each term to its meaning.

generalfeedback.text: Continuity is an unbroken path; an open is a complete break; a short is an unwanted path to ground; resistance is opposition to current, in ohms.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some pairs are wrong — open and short are opposites.

incorrectfeedback.text: Re-check: open = a break; short = an unwanted path to ground.

answer.text: an unbroken electrical path end to end
a complete break, so no current flows
an unwanted path, usually to ground
how strongly a path opposes the current

name.text: V3 · collocations — term to its usual word pair

questiontext.text: Match each term to the word it usually pairs with in maintenance documents.

generalfeedback.text: Learn the collocation with the word: a continuity test, a bonding strap, a shield braid, wire routing.

correctfeedback.text: All correct — these are the pairs used in the AMM and tech log.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some pairs are wrong — recall "continuity test" and "bonding strap".

incorrectfeedback.text: Re-check the usual pairs: continuity + test, bonding + strap.

name.text: V4 · structure terms — term to meaning

questiontext.text: Match each term to its meaning.

generalfeedback.text: The receptacle is the fixed half; the plug is the half you push in; a splice is a permanent joint; a terminal is a fixed connection point.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some pairs are wrong — plug vs receptacle is the key contrast.

incorrectfeedback.text: Re-check: receptacle = fixed half; plug = the half you push in.

answer.text: the fixed connector half, mounted on a unit
the connector half you push into the other
a joint where two conductors are joined
a point where a conductor is fixed
